title: Apify and Techi: why a non-coder needs a finished sample first
preview_markdown:
> Verdict
>
> - Use AI to leave an evidence trail an editor can inspect, not to make prose arrive faster.
> - A public writer application can care more about a readable sample, sources, and disclosures than follower counts.
> - One public program advertises $500 per accepted article. That is an opportunity, not a promise of payment.

At midnight, an unfinished draft has a familiar look. There are headings, a dozen tabs, and maybe a sharp opening paragraph. What it does not have is a clean answer to a basic question: which claim came from which source, and what can the reader do after finishing it?

For a writer who does not code, the useful first deliverable is not an AI tutorial. It is one article an editor can read and assess. Research, structure, the article, and its announcement belong around that single piece. A person still checks the final claims.

## What editors can actually inspect

Apify's public writer page advertises $500 per published article. It does not make acceptance automatic. The page is useful as a reminder that paid opportunities exist, not as a revenue forecast.

TECHi's public author application is clearer about the evidence it reviews: sample work, subject expertise, disclosures, and corroborated public profile material. It also says follower counts are not required. A finished sample can therefore do more work than a new social profile with nothing behind it.

Keep a small record beside the draft.

| Claim in the article | Evidence to retain | Final owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A payment or application condition | Official URL and date checked | Writer |
| A technical explanation | Primary source or official documentation | Writer |
| A recommendation | A sentence that marks it as judgment | Writer |

AI can help find candidates for that table. It cannot make the source support the claim. Open the link and check it before the claim enters the article.

## One article, one route through the work

Start with the outcome the reader needs. Here it is a submission-ready technical explainer, not a list of tools. Then give the reader a scene they recognize: an application form with a field for a work sample and no link worth pasting into it.

Build the draft in this order.

1. Read the publisher's public conditions and separate facts from hopes.
2. Choose one reader problem and write the claim in one sentence.
3. Explain the mechanism, then consolidate sources in one final list.
4. Write a separate short post that gives people one reason to return to the full article.

This is deliberately less exciting than asking an AI for an entire content machine. It is also more useful. A big stack can leave you with five drafts and no sample you would send to an editor.

## The review path

The draft gets stronger after evidence and disclosure are checked. Giving AI small jobs, such as locating source candidates or testing whether a heading is clear, also makes mistakes easier to trace.

## Before you submit

Check four things: every number has a source; personal experience is not blended with outside fact; the reader has one next action; and the publisher's disclosure policy has been read.

TECHi's editorial standards say software can speed research, draft checks, summaries, and edits, but does not replace reporting or editorial review. That boundary is sensible. When responsibility for the claim disappears, revision becomes guesswork.

Your first article does not need to prove an income. It needs to be a sample you can paste into an application. Sources, structure, and one useful route for the reader are enough to make the next revision concrete.

If you want to adapt this workflow to your own writing work, [see the article workflow](https://aniccaai.com/lm?product_id=anicca&run_id=20261018-194904&artifact_id=article-en&variant_id=finished-sample-first&click_id=20261018-194904-article-en).
